The charging schedule is similarly based on occupancy, where the baseline behavior assumes that the vehicle is plugged in when the occupant arrives home. In the figure, the charging availability schedule overlaps the occupancy schedule except for the time step where occupancy is partial (between 0 and 1). A partial occupancy time step, in which the occupant is home for only part of the 15-minute time step, would ideally reflect both charging and discharging. However, ResStock models these events entirely as discharging, as the underlying EnergyPlus® battery model can only be charged or discharged in a time step. This limitation may cut short or delay charging by up to 15 minutes; however, that is preferable to underestimating discharging, where events are shorter and changes in the duration would have a much larger impact on the total discharge energy—and, consequently, the charging energy. The charging availability schedule shown in the figure indicates when the vehicle is plugged in and eligible to be charged, whereas the actual charging, i.e., energy consumption, is handled by the battery model. Once charging begins, the only parameters that influence the timing and the magnitude of energy use are the charger power and the battery SOC. When charging availability schedule has a value of 1, the EV will charge at a constant power (5.69 kilowatts [Pavuluri 2024] 9 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. for L2 charger) until the maximum SOC is reached, at which point no further charging load occurs, regardless of the schedule. The behavior can be observed in Figure 3 prior to 10:30 and after 18:30 where charging power consumption remains zero despite charging availability schedule being 1. It can also be seen that the charging power remains constant at 5.69 kW when the vehicle is being charged – the slight depression during the second event where the charging power is below 5.69 kW is because in the underlying model charging doesn’t occur for the full 15 minutes before charging stops after reaching the maximum SOC. Electric Vehicle Modeling The charging availability and driving schedules are aligned with the stochastic occupancy model (based on American Time Use Survey data) in OpenStudio-HPXML. We calculate the total hours driven per week using the ev_average_mph (calculated from Federal Highway Administration [2022]) and ev_miles_per_year arguments from the “Electric Vehicle Battery” and “Annual Miles Driven” input files, respectively, which inform the charging and discharging schedule generation. The battery model takes care of the actual power draw during the charging and discharging periods. An example of what these schedules look like is presented in Figure 3. The charging schedule algorithm assumes that the occupant plugs in their vehicle as soon as they arrive home and keeps it plugged in until they leave. Thus, the charging availability schedule is identical to the occupancy schedule of the driver, but the schedule of actual charging typically differs.
